Ranking genotypes
For each year, the predicted and APSIM biomass of the 199 genotypes on a fixed day are compared by the Spearman correlation and by the overlap of the top 10%.

RPython


## Pd, Yd: genotype x year matrices of predicted and APSIM biomass on one
## day. For each year: Spearman correlation of the two rankings and overlap
## of the predicted and true top 10 %.
rank_scores <- function(Pd, Yd, top = 0.1) {
  k <- max(1, round(top * nrow(Yd)))
  score <- function(y) {
    overlap <- intersect(order(-Pd[, y])[1:k], order(-Yd[, y])[1:k])
    data.frame(year = y, rho = cor(Pd[, y], Yd[, y], method = "spearman"),
               top = length(overlap) / k)
  }
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(ncol(Yd)), score))
}


# Pd, Yd: genotype x year matrices of predicted and APSIM biomass on one
# day. For each year: Spearman correlation of the two rankings and overlap
# of the predicted and true top 10 %.
def rank_scores(Pd, Yd, top=0.1):
    from scipy.stats import spearmanr
    k = max(1, round(top * Yd.shape[0]))
    rho, overlap = [], []
    for s in range(Yd.shape[1]):
        rho.append(spearmanr(Pd[:, s], Yd[:, s])[0])
        best = set(np.argsort(-Pd[:, s])[:k]) & set(np.argsort(-Yd[:, s])[:k])
        overlap.append(len(best) / k)
    return np.array(rho), np.array(overlap)

title: 5 · Validation
text:
Solution
The fitted equation is solved with a standard ODE solver: deSolve::ode (LSODA) in R and scipy.integrate.solve_ivp (LSODA) in Python. All years are integrated in one call, each with its own coefficients. The solver needs the drivers at arbitrary times. Biomass is recorded at the end of a day, so the weather of day \(j\) drives the interval between observations \(j-1\) and \(j\). With \(t\) counted from the first observation, the value of day \(j\) is placed in the middle of that interval, \(t = j - \tfrac{3}{2}\), and values in between are interpolated linearly.

RPython


## Solves dy/dt = (1, theta(y, u)) coef. coef: year x (1 + terms), U: year
## x day x variable. terms(y, u) is the library; by default U is the library.
simulate <- function(coef, U, y0, terms = function(y, u) u, method = "lsoda") {
  S <- dim(U)[1]; D <- dim(U)[2]
  days <- lapply(seq_len(D), function(j) matrix(U[, j, ], S))
  b0 <- coef[, 1]; B <- coef[, -1, drop = FALSE]
  rhs <- function(t, y, parms) {
    pos <- min(max(t + 0.5, 0), D - 1)      # day j is placed at time j - 3/2
    j <- min(floor(pos), D - 2)
    w <- pos - j                            # linear interpolation between days
    u <- (1 - w) * days[[j + 1]] + w * days[[j + 2]]
    list(b0 + .rowSums(terms(y, u) * B, S, ncol(B)))
  }
  deSolve::ode(y0, 0:(D - 1), rhs, NULL, method = method, rtol = 1e-4,
               atol = 1e-4)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
}


# Solves dy/dt = (1, theta(y, u)) coef. coef: year x (1 + terms), U: year
# x day x variable. terms(y, u) is the library; by default U is the library.
def simulate(coef, U, y0, terms=lambda y, u: u, method="LSODA"):
    D = U.shape[1]

    def rhs(t, y):
        pos = min(max(t + 0.5, 0.0), D - 1.0)   # day j is placed at time j - 3/2
        j = min(int(pos), D - 2)
        w = pos - j                             # linear interpolation
        u = (1 - w) * U[:, j] + w * U[:, j + 1]
        return coef[:, 0] + np.einsum("sk,sk->s", terms(y, u), coef[:, 1:])

    return solve_ivp(rhs, (0, D - 1), y0, method=method, t_eval=np.arange(D),
                     rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4).y



If a library depends on the state, terms(y, u) is evaluated along the solution; by default the library depends on the drivers only.

title: 5 · Validation
text:
Leave-one-year-out cross-validation
Each genotype has trajectories in the years \(E\). A year \(e\) is predicted by a model that has not seen it:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\textbf{for each genotype } g, \textbf{ for each year } e \in E: & \\[2pt]
\quad \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(-e)} \leftarrow \texttt{fit}\bigl(\mathbf{X}^{(-e)},\, \dot{\mathbf{y}}^{(-e)}\bigr) & \text{fit on the other years} \\[2pt]
\quad \bar{y}_0^{(-e)} \leftarrow \tfrac{1}{|E|-1} \textstyle\sum_{e' \ne e} y_0^{(e')} & \text{mean initial biomass} \\[2pt]
\quad \dfrac{d\hat y}{dt} = \boldsymbol{\theta}\bigl(\mathbf{u}^{(e)}(t)\bigr)^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(-e)}, \quad \hat y(t_0) = \bar{y}_0^{(-e)} & \text{predict year } e \text{ from its drivers}
\end{array}
\]
Only the drivers of the left-out year enter the prediction. The error is the root-mean-square error (RMSE, t/ha) over whole trajectories, on a fixed day, and at maturity.

RPython


## Each year is predicted by a model fitted to the other years of the same
## genotype, starting from the mean initial biomass of those years.
## Returns P[genotype, year, day].
cross_validate <- function(Theta, tr, fit, genotypes = tr$genotypes) {
  P <- array(NA_real_, dim(tr$Y))
  S <- length(tr$years)
  for (g in match(genotypes, tr$genotypes)) {
    d <- make_design(Theta, tr, tr$genotypes[g])
    coef <- t(sapply(seq_len(S), function(v) {
      train <- d$year != v
      fit(d$X[train, ], d$dy[train])
    }))
    y0 <- (sum(tr$Y[g, , 1]) - tr$Y[g, , 1]) / (S - 1)
    P[g, , ] <- t(simulate(coef, Theta, y0))
  }
  P
}

## RMSE over whole trajectories, on a fixed day (array index; 99 is day 113
## after sowing) and at maturity. Genotypes that were not predicted are ignored.
evaluate <- function(P, tr, fixed_day = 99) {
  err <- P - tr$Y
  err[, , 1] <- NA                                # the initial value is given
  last <- cbind(as.vector(row(tr$nend)), as.vector(col(tr$nend)),
                as.vector(tr$nend) + 1)
  rmse <- function(e) sqrt(mean(e^2, na.rm = TRUE))
  c(trajectory_rmse = rmse(err), fixed_day_rmse = rmse(err[, , fixed_day]),
    maturity_rmse = rmse(err[last]))
}


# Each year is predicted by a model fitted to the other years of the same
# genotype, starting from the mean initial biomass of those years.
# Returns P[genotype, year, day].
def cross_validate(Theta, tr, fit, genotypes=None):
    P = np.full(tr.Y.shape, np.nan)
    S = len(tr.years)
    for g in (tr.genotypes if genotypes is None else genotypes):
        i = list(tr.genotypes).index(g)
        d = make_design(Theta, tr, g)
        coef = np.array([fit(d.X[d.year != s], d.dy[d.year != s])
                         for s in range(S)])
        y0 = (tr.Y[i, :, 0].sum() - tr.Y[i, :, 0]) / (S - 1)
        P[i] = simulate(coef, Theta.array, y0)
    return P


# RMSE over whole trajectories, on a fixed day (days after sowing) and at
# maturity. Genotypes that were not predicted are ignored.
def evaluate(P, tr, fixed_day=113):
    err = P - tr.Y
    err[:, :, 0] = np.nan                        # the initial value is given
    g, s = np.indices(tr.nend.shape)

    def rmse(e):
        return np.sqrt(np.nanmean(e ** 2))

    return {"trajectory_rmse": rmse(err),
            "fixed_day_rmse": rmse(err[:, :, fixed_day - tr.das0]),
            "maturity_rmse": rmse(err[g, s, tr.nend])}

title: 3 · Library and design matrix
text:
Drivers
The library is built from all eight variables of step 2, Tmin, Tmax, Rain, RAD, VP, DL, TT and RAW, standardised to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. They are denoted \(u_1, \dots, u_8\). A subset can be chosen with the argument drivers of make_drivers. The response does not enter this step.

RPython


make_drivers <- function(wx, drivers = c("Tmin", "Tmax", "Rain", "RAD", "VP", "DL",
                                          "TT", "RAW")) {
  years <- sort(unique(wx$year))
  das0 <- min(wx$das)
  nd <- max(wx$das) - das0 + 1
  U <- array(NA_real_, c(length(years), nd, length(drivers)),
             dimnames = list(years, NULL, drivers))
  for (j in seq_along(drivers)) {
    i <- cbind(match(wx$year, years), wx$das - das0 + 1, j)
    U[i] <- wx[[drivers[j]]]
  }
  # pad years that end early with their last value
  for (y in seq_along(years)) {
    for (j in seq_along(drivers)) {
      u <- U[y, , j]
      U[y, is.na(u), j] <- tail(u[!is.na(u)], 1)
    }
  }
  center <- apply(U, 3, mean)
  scale <- apply(U, 3, function(x) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2)))
  list(U = sweep(sweep(U, 3, center), 3, scale, "/"), years = years,
       das0 = das0, drivers = drivers, center = center, scale = scale)
}


def make_drivers(wx, drivers=DRIVERS):
    years = np.sort(wx["year"].unique())
    das0 = wx["das"].min()
    U = np.full((len(years), wx["das"].max() - das0 + 1, len(drivers)), np.nan)
    y = np.searchsorted(years, wx["year"])
    U[y, (wx["das"] - das0).to_numpy(), :] = wx[drivers].to_numpy()
    for s in range(len(years)):                  # years end on different days
        for j in range(len(drivers)):            # pad with the last value
            u = U[s, :, j]
            u[np.isnan(u)] = u[~np.isnan(u)][-1]
    center = U.mean(axis=(0, 1))
    scale = U.std(axis=(0, 1))
    return SimpleNamespace(U=(U - center) / scale, years=years, das0=das0,
                           drivers=list(drivers), center=center, scale=scale)

make_trajectories <- function(traj, drv, var = "biomass") {
  gen <- sort(unique(traj$genotype))

             dimnames = list(gen, drv$years, NULL))
  i <- cbind(match(traj$genotype, gen), match(traj$year, drv$years),
             traj$das - drv$das0 + 1)
  Y[i] <- traj[[var]]
  nend <- apply(Y, c(1, 2), function(v) sum(!is.na(v)) - 1)
  list(Y = Y, nend = nend, genotypes = gen, years = drv$years,
       das0 = drv$das0)
}

def make_trajectories(traj, drv, var="biomass"):
    genotypes = np.sort(traj["genotype"].unique())

    return SimpleNamespace(Y=Y, nend=(~np.isnan(Y)).sum(axis=2) - 1,

title: 3 · Library and design matrix
text:
Design matrix
For one genotype, the rows of \(\mathbf{X}\) are the observations of all years (all except the first and last of each) and the columns are the library terms; \(\dot{\mathbf{y}}\) holds the growth rates, estimated by the centered difference \((y_{i+1} - y_{i-1})/2\) (numpy.gradient and pracma::gradient). Biomass is recorded at the end of a day, so the weather of day \(i\) drives the change from observation \(i-1\) to \(i\); the library at observation \(i\) is the mean of the library values of days \(i\) and \(i+1\), the days on either side.



The regression problem for genotype g114 as a table: three days from the middle of each of the years 1, 2 and 31. The highlighted row is one equation, \(\dot y_i = \sum_j X_{ij}\xi_j\). The columns of \(\mathbf{X}\) are standardised; the coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) are unknown and are estimated in step 4.



RPython


## Rows: observations 2, ..., n of every year. dy: centered difference of the
## biomass. Biomass is recorded at the end of a day, so day i drives the change
## from observation i - 1 to i. X: library at observation i, the mean of the
## library of days i and i + 1.
make_design <- function(Theta, tr, genotype) {
  g <- match(genotype, tr$genotypes)
  n <- tr$nend[g, ]
  years <- seq_along(tr$years)
  X <- lapply(years, function(y)
    (Theta[y, 2:n[y], ] + Theta[y, 3:(n[y] + 1), ]) / 2)
  dy <- lapply(years, function(y)
    pracma::gradient(tr$Y[g, y, 1:(n[y] + 1)])[2:n[y]])
  X <- do.call(rbind, X)
  colnames(X) <- dimnames(Theta)[[3]]
  list(X = X, dy = unlist(dy), year = rep(years, n - 1))
}


# Rows: observations 2, ..., n of every year. dy: centered difference of the
# biomass. Biomass is recorded at the end of a day, so day i drives the change
# from observation i - 1 to i. X: library at observation i, the mean of the
# library of days i and i + 1.
def make_design(Theta, tr, genotype):
    g = list(tr.genotypes).index(genotype)
    n = tr.nend[g]
    years = range(len(tr.years))
    A = Theta.array
    X = np.vstack([(A[s, 1:n[s], :] + A[s, 2:n[s] + 1, :]) / 2 for s in years])
    dy = np.concatenate([np.gradient(tr.Y[g, s, :n[s] + 1])[1:n[s]]
                         for s in years])
    year = np.repeat(np.arange(len(tr.years)), n - 1)
    return SimpleNamespace(X=X, dy=dy, year=year, terms=Theta.terms)

title: 1 · Method
1 · Method
1 · Method
text:
Model
Let \(\mathbf{y}(t)\) denote the state of the crop (for example biomass or leaf area index) and \(\mathbf{u}(t) = (u_1(t), \dots, u_m(t))\) the environmental drivers. The growth of the crop is described by a system of ordinary differential equations:
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{y}}{dt} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u}).
\]
The growth rate \(r\) of one state variable \(y\) (a component of \(\mathbf{y}\), for example biomass) is expressed as a combination of candidate functions \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_K\) (the library),
\[
\frac{dy}{dt} = r(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u}) \approx \sum_{j=1}^{K} \xi_j\,\theta_j(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u}) = \boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u})^\top \boldsymbol{\xi},
\]
where most coefficients \(\xi_j\) are expected to be zero. The library contains candidate functions (inspired by crop physiology) that may be relevant to explain the growth rate. Furthermore, we can include flexible functions of the drivers, for example splines or polynomials, to capture unknown relationships. The coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) are estimated from the data by regression.



Schematic visualization of the methodology. Environmental drivers \(U\) and the crop state \(Y\) are measured over time. The estimated growth rate of \(Y\) is regressed on a library \(\Theta(Y, U)\) of candidate functions; a sparse coefficient matrix \(\Xi\) selects the terms of the equation. Figure from our preprint (Verburg, Heinlein, van Eeuwijk and Budko, 2026), Physiology-Informed Sparse Identification of Dynamic Crop Models.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Regression
Let \(y_i = y(t_i)\) be observations on days \(t_i\), with time step \(\Delta t\) (one day). The growth rate \(\dot y_i = \frac{dy}{dt}(t_i)\) is estimated by the centered difference
\[
\dot y_i \approx \frac{y_{i+1} - y_{i-1}}{2\,\Delta t}.
\]
Adding the Taylor expansions of \(y(t_i \pm \Delta t)\) in the form \(y_{i\pm1} = y_i \pm \Delta t\,\dot y_i + \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta t^2\,\ddot y_i \pm \dots\) shows that the error of the centered difference is of order \(\Delta t^2\), against order \(\Delta t\) for the forward difference \((y_{i+1} - y_i)/\Delta t\). The first and last observation of a trajectory have no neighbour on both sides and are not used. Routines for this are available in standard packages (numpy.gradient in Python, pracma::gradient in R).



Observed biomass of one genotype in one year (a). The box is enlarged in (b): the slope of the line through the observations on either side of day \(i\) estimates \(\dot y_i\). The growth rates of the whole year are shown in (c); the regression is performed on these.


Collecting all the growth rates in a vector \(\dot{\mathbf{y}}\) and the library values in a matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) with entries \(X_{ij} = \theta_j(\mathbf{y}_i, \mathbf{u}_i)\) gives
\[
\dot{\mathbf{y}} \approx \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\]
The state \(\mathbf{y}_i\) in the library is the observed state on day \(t_i\). If data are collected in several environments and for several genotypes, the growth rates and library values are stacked. With \(\theta_{i,j}^{(g, e)} = \theta_j(\mathbf{y}_i^{(g, e)}, \mathbf{u}_i^{(g, e)})\) for genotype \(g\) in environment \(e\) on day \(i\):
\[
{\small
\begin{pmatrix}
\dot y_1^{(1, 1)} \\ \vdots \\ \dot y_n^{(1, 1)} \\ \vdots \\ \dot y_n^{(g, e)}
\end{pmatrix}
\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
\theta_{1,1}^{(1, 1)} & \dots & \theta_{1,K}^{(1, 1)} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\theta_{n,1}^{(1, 1)} & \dots & \theta_{n,K}^{(1, 1)} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\theta_{n,1}^{(g, e)} & \dots & \theta_{n,K}^{(g, e)}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\xi_1 \\ \vdots \\ \xi_K
\end{pmatrix}
}
\]
The coefficients enter linearly (recall \(\dot{\mathbf{y}} \approx \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\xi}\)), so we just need to solve a linear regression problem to estimate them, for example by least squares:
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 .
\]
However, any regression method can be used. We will compare several methods in the workshop.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Making predictions
Given a fitted vector of coefficients \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\), the drivers \(\mathbf{u}(t)\) of a year and an initial state \(\mathbf{y}_0\), the state is predicted by solving the ODE with the estimated coefficients, using an ODE solver of our choice:
\[
\frac{dy}{dt} = \boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u})^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}, \qquad \mathbf{y}(t_0) = \mathbf{y}_0.
\]
If the library depends on the drivers only, the solution is the integral of the predicted growth rate, \(y(t) = y_0 + \int_{t_0}^t \boldsymbol{\theta}(\mathbf{u}(s))^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \, ds\), as in the figure.



Year 1998 of one genotype, predicted by a model fitted to the other years. With a library that depends on the drivers only, the predicted growth rate (a) is integrated from the initial value \(y_0\): the shaded area up to day \(t\) is the predicted increase in biomass, \(y(t) - y_0\) (b), which is compared with the APSIM trajectory.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Dealing with multiple genotypes
Differences between genotypes are captured by a separate regression for each genotype \(g = 1, \dots, G\), on its own growth rates and library values (stacked over the environments),
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(g)} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}}^{(g)} - \mathbf{X}^{(g)}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 .
\]
The environments and the library are shared, so the columns of \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Xi}} = \bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(1)}, \dots, \hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(G)}\bigr)\) are directly comparable: each column is the growth equation of one genotype, and the differences between columns describe how genotypes differ in their response to the drivers.

title: 1 · Method
text:
Validation
To test the predictive ability of the model, we can use leave-one-environment-out cross-validation. We calibrate the model on all but one environment, and then predict the left-out environment. This is repeated for each environment, and the predictions are compared with the observed values.



Leave-one-year-out cross-validation. Each row is one fit: the model is fitted to the years in blue and used to predict the left-out year in red.

title: Sparse identification of crop growth dynamics
text:
This workshop accompanies our preprint (Verburg, Heinlein, van Eeuwijk and Budko, 2026), Physiology-Informed Sparse Identification of Dynamic Crop Models. Constructed variables
Two further variables in the table are constructed from the weather variables: thermal time (TT) and relative available water (RAW).

  TT thermal time\(\sum_{s \le t} \max\left(\tfrac{T_{\min,s} + T_{\max,s}}{2}, 0\right)\)
  RAW relative available water\(W_t / W_{\max}\), bucket of rain and \(\mathrm{ET}_0\)

Thermal time measures the development of the crop. It is the cumulative sum of the thermal time of each day, the mean temperature truncated at zero:
\[
\mathrm{TT}_t = \sum_{s \le t} \max\left(\frac{T_{\min,s} + T_{\max,s}}{2},\, 0\right).
\]
The sum starts at sowing, so TT on the first day in the table (day 15) already contains the first 14 days.
Relative available water is the filling of a soil-water bucket: rain adds water and a fraction \(k\) of the reference evapotranspiration \(\mathrm{ET}_0\) removes it, up to the capacity \(W_{\max}\) of the soil,
\[
W_t = \min\bigl(\max(W_{t-1} + P_t - k\,\mathrm{ET}_{0,t},\, 0),\, W_{\max}\bigr), \qquad \mathrm{RAW}_t = \frac{W_t}{W_{\max}}.
\]
The capacity is the plant-available water capacity of the soil at Narrabri, \(W_{\max} = 217.5\) mm (a grey vertosol), and the bucket starts each season with the plant-available water at sowing, \(W_0 = 175\) mm, so that \(\mathrm{RAW}_0 = 0.80\) (Bustos-Korts et al., 2019, Table 1). \(\mathrm{ET}_0\) is the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith reference evapotranspiration, computed from the weather variables of the table, and \(k = 0.8\). With these values the bucket reproduces RAW over the whole season with an RMSE of 0.004.
In total there are eight variables: the six weather variables and the two constructed ones. All of them are candidates for the library.

title: 4 · Fitting
text:
This page continues from steps 2 and 3. One line loads the data and builds the library:
For one genotype, the data are the growth rates \(\dot{\mathbf{y}}\) and the library values \(\mathbf{X}\) of step 3, and the unknown is the coefficient vector \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\):
\[
\dot{\mathbf{y}} \approx \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\]
Every method maps \((\mathbf{X}, \dot{\mathbf{y}})\) to an estimate \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\), with the intercept first. A method is therefore a function fit(X, dy), and methods can be exchanged freely. Genotype g001 is used here.

title: 4 · Fitting
text:
Methods

Least squaresRidgeLassoElastic netBest subsetBackward eliminationSTLSQ


The reference: all terms are used, so there is no sparsity.
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2
\]
Hyperparameters: none.
R: lm.fit. Python: numpy.linalg.lstsq.

RPython


fit_ols <- function(X, dy) {
  Z <- cbind(`1` = 1, X)
  drop(solve(crossprod(Z), crossprod(Z, dy)))
}


def fit_ols(X, dy):
    return np.linalg.lstsq(np.column_stack([np.ones(len(dy)), X]), dy,
                           rcond=None)[0]





Shrinks the coefficients towards zero. Correlated terms share their weight, but none is removed.
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert \boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(\lambda\): strength of the penalty; shrinks the coefficients of correlated terms, but removes none.

Closed form, with the penalty scaled as in glmnet.

RPython


## Ridge in closed form, with the penalty scaling of glmnet.
fit_ridge <- function(X, dy, lambda = 1e-3) {
  n <- nrow(X); mx <- colMeans(X)
  var_x <- col_sd(X)^2 * (n - 1) / n
  sy <- sd(dy) * sqrt((n - 1) / n)
  b <- solve(crossprod(X) / n - tcrossprod(mx) + diag(lambda / sy * var_x),
             crossprod(X, dy) / n - mx * mean(dy))
  c(`1` = mean(dy) - sum(mx * b), setNames(drop(b), colnames(X)))
}


# Ridge: closed form, same scaling.
def fit_ridge(X, dy, lam=1e-3):
    sx = X.std(axis=0)
    Z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / sx
    A = Z.T @ Z / len(dy) + lam / dy.std() * np.eye(X.shape[1])
    b = np.linalg.solve(A, Z.T @ (dy - dy.mean()) / len(dy)) / sx
    return np.concatenate([[dy.mean() - X.mean(axis=0) @ b], b])





The \(\ell_1\) penalty sets coefficients exactly to zero, which gives a sparse equation.
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert \boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_1
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(\lambda\): strength of the penalty; larger values set more coefficients to zero.

R: glmnet. Python: scikit-learn ElasticNet, with the penalty scaled as in glmnet.

RPython


## Lasso and elastic net by glmnet.
fit_glmnet <- function(X, dy, alpha, lambda) {
  fit <- glmnet::glmnet(X, dy, alpha = alpha, lambda = lambda,
                        type.gaussian = "covariance")
  named(as.vector(coef(fit)), X)
}

fit_lasso <- function(X, dy, lambda = 3e-4) fit_glmnet(X, dy, 1, lambda)


# Lasso and elastic net, with the penalty scaling of glmnet.
def fit_glmnet(X, dy, alpha, lam):
    sx = X.std(axis=0)
    l1, l2 = lam * alpha, lam * (1 - alpha) / dy.std()
    model = ElasticNet(alpha=l1 + l2, l1_ratio=l1 / (l1 + l2), tol=1e-12,
                       max_iter=100000, precompute=True)
    model.fit((X - X.mean(axis=0)) / sx, dy - dy.mean())
    b = model.coef_ / sx
    return np.concatenate([[dy.mean() - X.mean(axis=0) @ b], b])


def fit_lasso(X, dy, lam=3e-4):
    return fit_glmnet(X, dy, 1, lam)





A mix of ridge and lasso: sparse like the lasso, but more stable for correlated terms.
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \Bigl( \tfrac{1 - \alpha}{2} \lVert \boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2 + \alpha \lVert \boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_1 \Bigr)
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(\lambda\): strength of the penalty.
\(\alpha\): mix of the two penalties (here 0.5); keeps groups of correlated terms together more readily than the lasso.

The best model with exactly \(k\) terms, found by searching all subsets.
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \arg\min_{\lVert \boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_0 \le k} \; \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(k\): number of terms that are kept.

R: leaps, which searches all subsets efficiently. Python: computed from the Gram matrix; with \(K = 24\) terms the exhaustive search takes about a second per fit, so it is left out of the comparison below.

RPython


## Best subset or backward elimination with k terms.
fit_subset <- function(X, dy, k = 8, method = "exhaustive") {
  b <- coef(leaps::regsubsets(X, dy, nvmax = k, method = method), k)
  full <- setNames(numeric(ncol(X) + 1), c("1", colnames(X)))
  full[c("1", names(b)[-1])] <- b
  full
}


# Best subset or backward elimination with k terms, from the Gram matrix.
def fit_subset(X, dy, k=8, method="exhaustive"):
    Xc, yc = X - X.mean(axis=0), dy - dy.mean()
    G, c = Xc.T @ Xc, Xc.T @ yc
    if method == "exhaustive":
        subsets = np.array(list(combinations(range(X.shape[1]), k)))
        blocks = G[subsets[:, :, None], subsets[:, None, :]]
        b = np.linalg.solve(blocks, c[subsets][..., None])[..., 0]
        keep = subsets[np.argmax((b * c[subsets]).sum(axis=1))]
    else:
        keep = np.arange(X.shape[1])
        while len(keep) > k:
            inv = np.linalg.inv(G[np.ix_(keep, keep)])
            increase = (inv @ c[keep]) ** 2 / np.diag(inv)
            keep = np.delete(keep, np.argmin(increase))
    b = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    b[keep] = np.linalg.solve(G[np.ix_(keep, keep)], c[keep])
    return np.concatenate([[dy.mean() - X.mean(axis=0) @ b], b])





A greedy alternative to best subset: start with all terms and repeatedly remove the one that increases the residual error least.
\[
S \leftarrow S \setminus \{j^*\}, \qquad j^* = \arg\min_{j \in S} \bigl[ \mathrm{RSS}(S \setminus \{j\}) - \mathrm{RSS}(S) \bigr]
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(k\): number of terms that are kept; terms are removed one at a time, starting from all \(K\) terms, until \(k\) remain.

The same function as best subset, called with method = "backward"; the cost grows only polynomially with the number of terms.

Sequential thresholded least squares, the algorithm of the original SINDy method.
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_S = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \lVert \dot{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{X}_S\boldsymbol{\xi} \rVert_2^2, \qquad S \leftarrow \bigl\{ j : |\hat{\xi}_j|\, s_j \ge \tau \bigr\}, \qquad s_j = \frac{\mathrm{sd}(\mathbf{X}_j)}{\mathrm{sd}(\dot{\mathbf{y}})}
\]
Hyperparameters:

\(\tau\): threshold on the scaled coefficient; the fit is repeated on the remaining terms until no term is removed (the algorithm of the original SINDy method).

Least squares on the active set \(S\), so there is no shrinkage.

RPython


## Sequential thresholded least squares: refit, drop terms below the threshold.
fit_stlsq <- function(X, dy, threshold = 0.05) {
  Z <- cbind(`1` = 1, X)
  G <- crossprod(Z)
  rhs <- drop(crossprod(Z, dy))
  size <- col_sd(X) / sd(dy)
  active <- colnames(X)
  repeat {
    i <- c("1", active)
    b <- drop(solve(G[i, i], rhs[i]))
    keep <- abs(b[-1]) * size[active] >= threshold
    if (all(keep) || !any(keep)) break
    active <- active[keep]
  }
  full <- setNames(numeric(ncol(X) + 1), c("1", colnames(X)))
  full[names(b)] <- b
  full
}


# Sequential thresholded least squares: refit, drop terms below the threshold.
def fit_stlsq(X, dy, threshold=0.05):
    size = X.std(axis=0, ddof=1) / dy.std(ddof=1)
    active = np.arange(X.shape[1])
    while True:
        b = fit_ols(X[:, active], dy)
        keep = np.abs(b[1:]) * size[active] >= threshold
        if keep.all() or not keep.any():
            break
        active = active[keep]
    full = np.zeros(X.shape[1] + 1)
    full[0], full[1 + active] = b[0], b[1:]
    return full

predictor <- function(coef, pairs = FALSE) {
  rate <- function(model, newdata) {
    L <- library_matrix(as.matrix(newdata), pairs = pairs)
    as.vector(cbind(1, L) %*% model)
  }
  Predictor$new(coef, data = Z, predict.function = rate)
}

             x = natural(effect[[drv$drivers[j]]], j), effect = effect$.value)
}

title: 6 · Interpretation
text:
Interactions and partial dependence
The library of powers is additive in the drivers: the effect of one driver does not depend on the others, and ALE and partial dependence coincide. With products of pairs of drivers (136 terms, backward elimination to 20 terms) they differ. For g114, partial dependence averages the growth rate over all observed days while one driver is set to each value in turn.

RPython



Theta2 <- make_library(drv, pairs = TRUE)
d2 <- make_design(Theta2, tr, "g114")
pred2 <- predictor(fit_subset(d2$X, d2$dy, k = 20, method = "backward"), TRUE)

effects <- function(j) {
  feature <- drv$drivers[j]
  ale <- FeatureEffect$new(pred2, feature, "ale", grid.size = 24)$results
  pdp <- FeatureEffect$new(pred2, feature, "pdp", grid.size = 24)$results
  pdp$x <- natural(pdp[[feature]], j)
  pdp$driver <- factor(feature, drv$drivers)
  pdp$.value <- pdp$.value - mean(pdp$.value)
  ale$x <- natural(ale[[feature]], j)
  ale$driver <- pdp$driver[1]
  pdp[[feature]] <- NULL
  ale[[feature]] <- NULL
  list(pdp = pdp, ale = ale)
}
parts <- lapply(1:2, effects)



Theta2 = make_library(drv, pairs=True)
d2 = make_design(Theta2, tr, "g114")
rate2 = GrowthRate(fit_subset(d2.X, d2.dy, k=20, method="backward"), pairs=True)

def effects(feature):
    j = drv.drivers.index(feature)
    a = ale(Z, rate2, [feature], grid_size=24, include_CI=False, plot=False)
    grid = np.linspace(Z[feature].min(), Z[feature].max(), 24)
    pdp = np.array([rate2.predict(Z.assign(**{feature: v})).mean()
                    for v in grid])
    return (natural(grid, j), pdp - pdp.mean(),
            natural(a.index.to_numpy(), j), a["eff"].to_numpy())

    x, pdp, xa, a = effects(feature)
    ax.plot(x, pdp, color=BURGUNDY, lw=1.5, label="partial dependence")
    ax.plot(xa, a, "--", color=BLUE, lw=1.5, label="ALE")
    ax.set_title(feature, loc="left")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
fig.supxlabel("driver value")
fig.supylabel("effect on growth rate (t/ha/day)")

The two curves differ because of the interactions. Partial dependence also evaluates the model at combinations of drivers that do not occur in the data, for example a short day late in a year with high thermal time, whereas ALE does not.
